subject: The Papyrus · The virus Egypt was losing to — and then beat
html:
A public-health number that almost never happens

Most health statistics move slowly. This one didn't. In 2016 roughly 10% of Egyptians were living with hepatitis C — the highest national rate in the world. By 2023 that had fallen to about 0.38%. A country went from the global worst to the edge of elimination in seven years. (Source: WHO, 9 Oct 2023.)

How the virus got there is its own data story: it spread decades earlier partly through mass public-health campaigns that reused needles — a hard lesson in how the tools meant to cure can also carry disease. By the 2010s it was a slow national emergency, quietly filling liver wards.

What changed

Between 2018 and 2019 Egypt ran “100 Million Seha” (100 Million Healthy Lives) — screening on a scale rarely attempted anywhere. Roughly 60 million adults were tested in about a year, and everyone who tested positive was offered treatment with locally manufactured direct-acting antivirals, which cut the price of a cure from thousands of dollars to a fraction of that. (Sources: WHO; Egypt Ministry of Health & Population.)

In October 2023 the WHO validated Egypt at “gold tier” on the path to eliminating hepatitis C — the first country in the world to reach that bar. (Source: WHO, 9 Oct 2023.)

Why it matters to a data person

Both of those numbers — the 10% in 2016 and the 0.38% in 2023 — sit in EgyBI's indicators table right now, cited to that same WHO source. A prevalence that falls by a factor of about 26× is exactly the kind of thing a single line of SQL can make you feel: query the two rows, take the ratio, and the scale of it lands harder than any headline.

See it charted →  ·  Query the numbers yourself →

One country, one virus, one campaign, and a number that moved the way numbers almost never do. See you next month.
